articles.title_orig: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.title_zh: US 30-year mortgage rate hits highest in nearly three years
articles.content_orig:
Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home more challenging at a time when housing prices are already high. Nam Y. Huh/AP hide caption
Carrie Goldstein's dream for a new home started with a family reunion at her cousin's home in Milwaukee. The home was old with character and she could walk anywhere from the front door.
"We were kind of in awe and drooling over her walkability," Goldstein says.
It was the lifestyle Goldstein wanted but lacked in her Cleveland suburb, which she says is also pretty walkable – with one major issue.
"There are lots of sidewalks," she says. "But you can't really go anywhere."
She brainstormed with her husband and realized nearby Rocky River was where they wanted to live. It was still a suburb, but with a quaint downtown and the option to walk to Lake Erie.
But as much as she wanted to move, one thing stopped her cold. The mortgage she would have to pay. Mortgage rates have hit their highest level in almost three years, making buying a home impossible for many people at a time when housing prices are also sky high.
Goldstein is running into a problem that's affecting many households at a time when people have already been struggling with years of high inflation: The rising cost of borrowing.
Carrie Goldstein stands outside her home on October 4, 2026. Home prices and mortgage rates prevent her from moving. Mike Goldstein hide caption
Bond markets influence all types of borrowing costs across the economy – and as yields have surged to their highest in decades, they've pushed up all kinds of interest rates paid by consumers, from loans for homes to cars and higher education.
And those rates are likely to continue moving up after the Federal Reserve in September raised interest rates for the first time this year – while signaling an additional hike could come this year.
Rate hikes from the Federal Reserve filter through the economy and are meant to slow down consumer and business spending by making people hesitant to take out a more expensive loan to pay for a car or a home – both essential purchases for many people.
"If you need to borrow, boy, it's really not a good time," says John Diamond, senior director of the Center for Tax and Budget Policy at the Baker Institute.
Buying a home is a key example of how households are affected when borrowing costs rise in the economy.
While mortgage rates were falling at the start of this year, they reversed upward after the U.S. war with Iran spooked the bond market by raising worries about inflation. As a result, mortgage rates, which are influenced by the bond markets, have surged this year.
For example, at the current 7.28% level for the average 30-year fixed rate mortgage, a person could end up paying about $900 more a month compared with the 3% pandemic-era rates for a median priced home.
As expected, fewer homeowners are willing or capable of making that financial leap, even if they have long since outgrown their current home. Existing house sales in August were down about 1.2% from a year earlier, according to the National Association of Realtors.
It's not just mortgage costs that are making Americans like Goldstein wince.
Alongside her dreams of owning a home in a walkable neighborhood, Goldstein is ready for a new car. Her old one is 11 years old, has 150,000 miles and plenty of quirks. The repair costs are approaching the point where they'll be more than the value of the actual car.
But a four-year loan for a used car is about three percentage points higher compared with the start of 2022, right around when auto loans began to shed their pandemic-era low rates and started climbing up.
"You can't go and get a car for $150 or $180 bucks anymore a month," she says about the car payments she would be facing.
Although so far the Fed has only delivered a modest quarter of a percentage point, it's adding to the higher borrowing costs at a time when households are already dealing with inflation and higher prices for other types of borrowing.
"It's added to higher mortgage payments. Higher student loan payments. Higher prices because of inflation," Diamond says. "That's what makes it really painful."
And that could mean that households could continue to delay any big purchases requiring a loan.
Goldstein is one of them. She says she can afford to wait on the car and house. But eventually she unsubscribed from real estate updates for that walkable suburb.
"It just became more and more disheartening when I did the math," Goldstein says. "It's just not in the cards."

articles.title_orig: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.title_zh: A UMass study has revealed two of the world’s loudest birds. Here’s what they sound like.
articles.content_orig:
Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories.
University of Massachusetts Amherst biologists have discovered two contenders for the world’s loudest birds, both from Brazil.
The bare-throated bellbird and the red-legged seriema are louder than jackhammers and may just be the loudest birds in the world, according to a study published in Evolution by UMass professor Jeff Podos and his former graduate student João Menezes.
This isn’t the first groundbreaking discovery for Podos. In fact, his research established a Guinness World Record in 2019 when he discovered that the Amazon’s white bellbird had the world’s loudest bird call, louder than a revving chainsaw.
The latest discovery is the result of Podos and Menezes’s years of ongoing research to understand the role evolutionary biology plays in how birds communicate with each other. Their research aims to solve the mystery of why some birds are so much louder than others, and whether there are certain physical traits that can predict their volume.
Menezes said it’s difficult to measure how loud a bird call is in the field, and there’s little data available. But using cutting-edge tools, Podos and Menezes have gathered reliable amplitude data on 123 species throughout Massachusetts and Brazil, 113 of which had never before had their volume catalogued.
“We’ve been able to vastly increase the number of species for which there is amplitude data,” Podos said. “This is basic, foundational research that no one else has managed to do on this scale, and it points to all sorts of other questions that would be fun to follow up.”
Podos and Menezes discovered there’s a 58-decibel range in the volume of bird calls, from the hummingbird, whose calls are 64 decibels and about the volume of a normal conversation, to bare-throated bellbirds and red-legged seriemas, who register at over 120 decibels.
They found that the loudest birds are typically bigger, with wider beak openings and bulky muscles that may allow greater air compression for explosive volume. But Podos and Menezes said there’s still a lot unknown about how birds communicate.
“We now know some of the hows,” Menezes said. “Bigger bodies and wider beaks. But we’ve yet to discover the whys, and we probably need much more data from many more species to be able to tease out what’s going on on the ecological and evolutionary front.”

articles.title_orig: Space station crew heads home as replacements settle in for 6-month tour of duty
articles.title_zh: Space station crew heads home as replacements settle in for 6-month tour of duty
articles.content_orig:
The four people departing the International Space Station strapped into their Crew Dragon capsule and undocked early Wednesday, setting up re-entry and splashdown Thursday off the coast of Southern California to close out a 237-day stay in orbit.
With Crew 12 commander Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway at the controls, flanked on their left by European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot and on the right by cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, the Crew Dragon "Freedom" backed away from the space-facing port on the forward Harmony module at 8:05 a.m. Eastern Time.
Sailing 260 miles above Cuba and the Bahamas, the capsule executed an automated loop over the top of the lab complex and slowly dropped away behind, exiting the safety zones around the station.
"We just wanted to give an enormous thank you to all of the team, our friends and colleagues on board the International Space Station, everybody in Houston, everybody at SpaceX, all around the world, with all of our international partners," Meir radioed as the Crew Dragon departed. "We have had the most incredible of expeditions ... and we will never forget it, and never forget all of your hard work."
After enjoying a final day in weightlessness, Meir and Hathaway will monitor a nine-minute and 20-second firing of the Crew Dragon's forward Draco thrusters starting at 10:46 a.m. ET on Thursday, setting up a fiery plunge back to Earth and splashdown off the coast of California at 11:34 a.m. ET.
Left behind aboard the space station were the Crew 13 fliers that replaced them — commander Jessica Watkins, pilot Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov — who were launched to the station on Oct. 1.
Also on board are Soyuz MS-29 commander Pyotr Dubrov, cosmonaut Anna Kikina and NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan on July 14. They plan to remain aboard the station for eight months while Crew 13 is planning a six-month tour of duty.
In a brief ceremony Sunday, Meir turned command of the station over to Dubrov, saying Crew 12's departure would mark a "bittersweet" moment.
"We will be leaving our friends," she said. "But we know that we are going home to our friends, to our families, to all of our team members on the ground. So it's a lot of mixed, swirling emotions for all of us when one leaves a home like this up on the space station."
She presented a symbolic "key to the space station" to Dubrov, who said "it's a great honor and a great responsibility to be the commander of such a magnificent place like International Space Station."
"It has a special meaning for me today, because 69 years ago on this day (Oct. 4) the first Sputnik was launched. Today is the dawn of the space era for humanity, and International Space Station is the greatest symbol of what we can do if we work together."
The combined crews then gathered in a group hug, or "huggle," as Meir described it, forming a circle with arms around each other's shoulders.
With splashdown Thursday, Meir, Hathaway, Adenot and Fedyaev will wrap up a 237-day and five-hour mission, flying around the planet 3,792 times and logging nearly 101 million miles from start to finish.
Meir, wrapping up her second flight to the space station, will have logged a total of 442 days in space, completing four spacewalks during the Crew 12 mission and three during an earlier stay. Adenot carried out three back-to-back spacewalks of her own, including one with Meir and two with Menon.

articles.title_orig: Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges
articles.title_zh: Germany: Ex-spy chief sent to pretrial detention on treason charges
articles.content_orig:
Former German foreign intelligence agency boss August Hanning appeared before a federal judge in the western city of Karlsruhe on Wednesday following his arrest on espionage and treason charges Tuesday.
He has been ordered to remain in detention ahead of his trial, according to federal prosecutors.
Manfred D., Hanning's former chief of staff at the Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) , was also detained.
Manfred D. is accused of having stolen secret documents and turned these over to Hanning, who, as a private-sector security adviser, in turn reportedly sold the secret documents to an as yet unnamed foreign spy agency or agencies.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Investigators estimate the two stole and potentially passed on more than 2,000 secret documents between 2010 and 2023. Federal investigators say it is unclear how much information was stolen and to whom it was sold.
Hanning ran the BND, Germany's foreign intelligence service, from 1998 until 2005 before becoming state secretary at the Federal Interior Ministry and then entering private business as a security adviser.
The issue has raised serious questions about the trustworthiness of Germany's intelligence agencies and shocked politicians into action as they claim not enough is being done to ensure high-ranking officials do not abuse their experience when transitioning to jobs in the private sector.
Although it is currently not known who Hanning's potential customers were, Germany's weekly Der Spiegel magazine on Wednesday named Azerbaijan as one. The Azerbaijan Media and Broadcasting Council vehemently denied the accusation, calling it "unfounded" and adding, "The malicious intent of the ‌forces behind this disinformation operation is ‌to ​damage Azerbaijan-Germany relations."

articles.title_orig: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.title_zh: 11 Places to See the World's Most Magnificent Wildlife Migrations
articles.content_orig:
Seeing an immense number  of creatures assembled in one place is a phenomenon worth travelling for. Here’s when, where and how to experience some of nature’s wildest gatherings.
Seeing any animal in the wild is a privilege — but seeing huge numbers is something else. For a start, it’s both humbling and heartening to encounter any species in abundance. It’s also genuinely exciting. When big groups of creatures seasonally cluster in one place, there’s always something to watch — from courting and mating to fighting or family-raising. It may be a sensory assault, too: noise, tumult, pungent smells, crashing waters, mad flurries of dust. And where masses gather to move together, hungry predators may lurk, adding a macabre but fascinating dimension. Here, we’ve picked the most dramatic migrations through the year and around the globe.
When to go: December to March
How does an insect the weight of a paperclip make a journey of 3,000 miles? That’s the feat of the extraordinary monarch butterfly, which somehow flutters from its summer breeding grounds — spread across Canada and the American northeast — to a patch of oyamel fir forest in the highlands west of Mexico City. Most only survive for a month or so but, in autumn, a generation emerges that lives eight times as long, capable of making this perilous trip. How they know where to go is a mystery — the butterflies that migrate are the great-great-grandchildren of those that left Mexico the previous spring. No matter, the results are spectacular: millions upon millions of orange-black wings blanketing trees, raining like tickertape. The Monarch Butterfly Biosphere Reserve, in the mountains of Michoacán state, is home to more than half of the overwintering colonies of the monarch butterfly’s eastern population. The sanctuary of El Rosario is easiest to reach; lesser-visited Sierra Chincua can be explored on horseback. The colourful, cobblestoned Mineral de Angangueo makes a good base.
The Indigenous Sámi of Europe’s far north work to their own calendar. Their year has eight seasons, and giđđa (spring) means melting snows, fast-increasing daylight and reindeer on the move: around April, the animals start migrating from their inland pastures towards the coast for summer grazing. Norway has around 275,000 reindeer, some wild, but mostly semi-domesticated herds that are ushered across the country’s Arctic plateaus by Sámi families whose livelihoods have depended on the practice for generations. Finnmarksvidda, an empty vastness of low hills, glacial lakes, pine barrens, birch woods and bogs in northernmost Norway, is a Sámi stronghold, where a few operators offer the chance to join the herders on the move. Days are shaped by the reindeer and the weather, perhaps involving sledding, snowmobiling or feeding the animals, followed by sharing stories around the fire, feasting on Arctic fish and sleeping in lavvus (traditional tents). Seeing swathes of animals trot across the tundra is a treat; being immersed in Sámi culture is an even greater privilege.
A strange thing happens off the South African coast each winter in the Southern Hemisphere: sardines in their millions, maybe billions, swarm north from Cape Agulhas, following a cold current towards the Indian Ocean. Strange, because it doesn’t benefit the sardines at all. But it’s a bumper buffet for other creatures: dolphins, tuna, seals, sharks, orcas and whales, plus dive-bombing cormorants, gannets and gulls. The result is marine mayhem. The sardines become silvery shape-shifting bait balls, chased down by great gangs of hungry predators and pierced by an avian invasion from above. Fish numbers have plunged in recent decades and the Sardine Run has become less predictable, but it’s still known as one of Earth’s greatest shoals. Activity peaks off Eastern Cape province, with boat trips leaving from towns such as Port St Johns and Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth, handy for Addo Elephant National Park, too). Diving amid this chaos is thrilling, if challenging; snorkellers can launch into the action more quickly. Or, stay on board to watch the feasting frenzy from above.
With their massive bills and bodies, capacious pouches and wide, powerful wings, pelicans look both immensely impressive and distinctly prehistoric. Come spring, around 32,000 of them — mostly great whites, plus a significant scoop of dalmatians, the biggest species — leave their winter hangouts and make for Europe’s largest natural wetland, the Danube Delta. This splurge of rivers, lakes, marshes, forest, sandbars and reedbeds spreads mostly across eastern Romania. It’s a paradise for the pelicans, as well as other birds such as herons, storks and white-tailed eagles. The pelicans begin arriving in March, but May is an ideal time to visit, when colonies are a-bustle, large pods gather for herd-fishing and adults are in full breeding splendour, their great gular pouches beaming bright-orange. June, on the other hand, is good for spying chicks, and July the time to go for sheer numbers. Navigate the delta on boat trips with licensed guides (mandatory for exploring core areas) or stay on a floating hotel for 24/7 avian action.
When to go: July to October
No migration is easy, but the journey of the Pacific Northwest salmon reads like a Greek tragedy. Born in fresh water, they head out to sea, mature for a few years, then navigate back to their natal streams using the earth’s magnetic fields and their own sense of smell. They battle against the flow, leaping rapids, dodging grizzlies and eagles, only to spawn — and then die. It’s a privilege to witness this fatal journey, either from the riverbank, as the fish fling themselves from the froth, or in the water amid the shoals. The town of Campbell River, on Vancouver Island’s east coast, is the self-proclaimed ‘salmon capital of the world’, and the top spot for snorkelling with the chinook, coho, chum, pink and sockeye fighting to return home. Floating in the swift current, you might see hundreds, even thousands, of salmon swim past — and possibly some bears hanging about. From the banks, you can watch salmon leaping two metres into the air, perhaps only to be snatched by those waiting bears. From mid-August to late October, the Homalco First Nation run bear-watching trips to Bute Inlet.
When to go: October to December
The wildebeest in Kenya and Tanzania might grab the headlines, but the world’s biggest mammal migration happens further south. Kasanka National Park is one of Zambia’s smallest and, come October, around 10 million straw-coloured fruit bats overwhelm the remote enclave. By day, they weigh down the trees, wrapped snugly amid  the leaves. But at dusk they take flight, creating a deafening, whirling maelstrom of leathery wings as they seek supper — the bats weigh around 250g and can consume the same in fruit every night. At dawn they return, the maelstrom in reverse.  A good 10-hour drive from the capital of Lusaka, Kasanka National Park is offbeat, but tree hides and viewing platforms ensure the safari-goers who do make the effort get front-row seats. And it isn’t just bats: 114 mammal species have been recorded, from elephant to sitatunga antelope, plus 450 bird species. A trip here combines well with relatively nearby South Luangwa National Park, home to prolific wildlife and pioneering walking safaris.
When to go: June to October
Sea turtles: so cumbersome on land, so graceful underwater. These reptiles swim vast distances across oceans but must return to shore — back to the beach where they were born — to nest. There are seven species worldwide, five have nesting grounds in Costa Rica. Unsurprisingly, given its name is derived from ‘ tortuga ’ — the Spanish word for ‘turtle’ — Tortuguero is a hotspot. This national park on the country’s Caribbean coast is home to the western hemisphere’s largest green turtle rookery, as well as significant populations of leatherbacks and hawksbills.

articles.title_orig: Israelis mourn Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza languish in ruins of the war it sparked
articles.title_zh: Israelis mourn Oct. 7 attack as Palestinians in Gaza languish in ruins of the war it sparked
articles.content_orig:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lays a wreath during a state memorial ceremony in memory of those killed in the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack on Israel, at Mount Herzl cemetery in Jerusalem on Oct. 5. Debbie Hill/Pool UPI via AP hide caption
TEL AVIV, Israel — As Israel marks three years since Hamas launched its surprise Oct. 7 attacks, Israelis are reeling from new revelations in Israeli and U.S. media that the country had been repeatedly warned by its regional allies that Hamas was planning to attack.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was personally warned about a potential Hamas attack, and his security agencies were notified repeatedly, in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023, four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR.
The Israeli newspaper Haaretz , The New York Times and The Atlantic first reported about the warnings.
Netanyahu has denied he was warned, calling the reports "fake news" and filing a defamation lawsuit last week against Israeli news outlets that published them. He and his defense minister have issued new warnings that Hamas could try to attack or "challenge" Israel on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to national elections later this month.
But the Oct. 7, 2023, security failure — as well as Netanyahu's repeated refusal to take responsibility for it — has become a lightning rod in Israel as the prime minister seeks a new term in national elections this month.
"You didn't protect my son," yelled out one bereaved Israeli father whose son was killed in the Hamas-led attack, as the prime minister spoke at a memorial ceremony this week for the victims.
One warning came directly from the leader of Hamas in Gaza weeks before Oct. 7, a Palestinian mediator told NPR and other media outlets.
Former Palestinian Authority official Sufian Abu Zaida said he helped mediate secret Hamas-Israel talks for more than a year leading up to Oct. 7. He said Hamas wanted Israel to release Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and offered in exchange to release two living Israeli hostages and the bodies of two Israeli soldiers held in Gaza for years. But he said Israel was unwilling to release as many prisoners as Hamas had demanded.
On Sept. 14, 2023, Abu Zaida said, Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar dictated a message for him to deliver to Israel: "By the end of September, we will put cards on the table. There will be an earthquake in the negotiations, and the Israelis should prepare to empty their prisons."
He did not know what kind of earthquake Sinwar meant, but he said he sent the message to an Israeli intelligence official who acknowledged receiving it and to Mohammed Dahlan, a Palestinian confidant of the leader of the United Arab Emirates.
"What happened [on] the 7th of October is needless," Abu Zaida told NPR.
Days before the Oct. 7 attacks, the leader of the United Arab Emirates, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, called Netanyahu and told him that Hamas' leader in Gaza was planning a big assault against Israel, according to a person close to Dahlan. Dahlan was the Palestinian Authority's head of security in Gaza before Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007.
The Emirati leader told Netanyahu in a phone call that lasted more than 40 minutes that a "quake" would hit the region if no progress was achieved regarding a prisoner deal between Hamas and Israel, the person said.
The person spoke to NPR on condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the call. The phone call was previously reported by Haaretz and The New York Times .
The UAE did not deny the report, saying only that it maintained dialogue with Israel.
People visit a memorial at a police station attacked by Hamas on Oct. 7, 2023, three years prior, in Sderot, southern Israel, on Oct. 4. Oded Balilty/AP hide caption
A senior Egyptian official told NPR that Egypt had specific intelligence about Hamas movements and that Egypt's head of intelligence at the time, Abbas Kamel, had traveled to Israel with two other senior officials and met with Israel's Mossad and Shin Bet intelligence chiefs.
The official said Kamel relayed a warning that Gaza was on the verge of an "explosion" because of Israel's blockade, the condition of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and concerns that Israel might move to annex the occupied West Bank.
The official was not authorized to speak publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity. The Atlantic reported that Kamel's visit to Israel was on Sept 26.
Nimrod Novik, a fellow at the Israel Policy Forum think tank and a former top adviser to late Israeli Prime Minister Shimon Peres, told NPR that he was informed before Oct. 7 by a person with firsthand knowledge that Egypt had delivered warnings to several senior Israeli officials that "Gaza is about to explode in your face."
Novik said one warning was an "urgent and dramatic message" from Egypt, delivered to a person close to Netanyahu some 10 days prior to Oct. 7.
"I'm certain that the issue of the early warnings on October 7 is going to continue to play with heightened emotions as we approach Election Day," said Novik. "This is going to be an indictment for history, not just for the elections."
Netanyahu has blamed Israeli security organizations for failing to stop the Oct. 7 attacks. He and his government have yet to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the failures around Oct. 7, despite public demand.
The new reports about warnings issued to Israel "actually turn the story on its head," pointing the finger right back at the prime minister, said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
"It violates the basic narrative that Netanyahu tries to tell Israelis," said Talshir.
NPR's Aya Batrawy contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Atmosfy Launches Atlas to Power AI's View of the Real World
articles.content_orig:
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct. 7, 2026
Built on the world's largest live video map, Atlas turns authentic video into real-world intelligence for AI, search and commerce.
SAN FRANCISCO , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Atmosfy today announced Atlas, a platform that gives AI a live view of the physical world. Atlas is built on Atmosfy , the world's largest live video map, with more than 500 million experiences spanning 100 million places across 20,000 cities in 150 countries.
The video map is powered by Atmosfy's global community, capturing moments at restaurants, bars, hotels, stadiums and other places around the world. Each video connects a real place to a moment in time.
Spectra, Atlas's latest intelligence model, turns those videos into time capsules, connecting them into a single, living picture of the world.
Building on existing partnerships with Capital One, Expedia, SeatGeek, GetYourGuide, Virgin Hotels, Resy, Funko and others, Atmosfy is expanding through Atlas into video and data licensing for frontier AI models.
"As AI takes on more decisions for people, it needs to understand what's happening in the real world," said Michael Ebel, Founder and CEO of Atmosfy. "Where to go, what to book, what to recommend: those decisions depend on how places and experiences are changing. Atlas gives AI a continuously updated view of that world."
Atmosfy is the "what's happening" app for millennials and Gen Z. Its global community maps what's happening across 20,000 cities through real-world video, creating city-based feeds that show where people are going and what they're doing right now.
Atmosfy is backed by Redpoint Ventures, Capital One Ventures, Canaan Partners, Industry Ventures, Streamlined Ventures, DNX Ventures, Suntory Ventures, Plug and Play, and others. See Atlas in action at atmosfy.io .
Michael Ebel Founder and CEO, Atmosfy michael@atmosfy.io

articles.title_orig: German ex-spy chief arrested for treason: What we know
articles.title_zh: German ex-spy chief arrested for treason: What we know
articles.content_orig:
The man who led Germany’s intelligence agency from 1998 to 2005 has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and attempted treason, according to the country’s federal prosecutor’s office.
The office announced on Tuesday that August Hanning, 80, was arrested and faces charges including “treasonous espionage, obtaining state secrets, attempted treason” through contact with foreign intelligence services.
The office has not specified which country or countries Hanning is accused of working for.
Citing unnamed sources, however, German news outlet Der Spiegel reported that Hanning was in contact with an Azerbaijan intelligence agency representative. In 2025, prosecutors also accused Hanning of ties with Israeli spies in a separate case which ultimately led them to the ex-intelligence boss’s alleged espionage for other agencies.
If found guilty, treason carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment in Germany.
German news outlet Deutsche Welle described Hanning’s arrest as Germany’s “biggest espionage scandal of the century”.
Born in Nordwalde, Westphalia, western Germany, in 1946, Hanning served as the head of the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and later moved to work in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, before working as a state secretary until 2009.
He later worked as a private consultant.
German media showed pictures of Hanning being taken from his red-brick house in Norwalde, close to Munster, to a bulletproof vehicle by masked officers on Tuesday morning.
They claim Hanning used classified intelligence to “draft an analysis” for a foreign intelligence service and kept “close contact” with another foreign spying service for “several years” while he was working as a private consultant.
They say that in 2010, Hanning came to an agreement to receive confidential information from his former bureau chief – who was in office until March this year and is named only as “Manfred D” – and was preparing to provide an “analysis” of it to a foreign power in exchange for money. It is unclear if the analysis was duly shared.
However, Hanning is also alleged to have passed on potentially sensitive political information, partly based on information provided by Manfred D, to a contact representing a separate foreign intelligence service.
Manfred D was also arrested on Tuesday and charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.
“Both suspects are believed to have agreed, in the spring of 2010, to have Manfred D continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the Federal Intelligence Service to Hanning in exchange for remuneration,” a statement from the prosecutor’s office said.
Over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, “many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings”, it added.
“Hanning was to capitalise on said information in the context of his private consulting services, which he had since been offering,” the prosecutor’s office said.
The alleged espionage by Hanning and Manfred D was uncovered during an investigation into a separate kidnapping case involving German businesswoman and steakhouse chain heiress, Christina Block.
In that case, Hamburg prosecutors accused Block of arranging the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Prosecutors said Hanning put Block in touch with a private Israeli espionage firm to carry out the abductions. The former spy chief and a police officer were accused of accepting more than 100,000 euros ($112,000) from Block in exchange for returning her children from Denmark, where they were living with her ex-husband. The trial is ongoing.
Little detail is available about the contents of the 2,000 documents, but German news outlet Suddeutsche Zeitung reported that a number of them related to Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military.
It added that other materials were highly sensitive and classified as secret by allied intelligence agencies in other countries.
Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said in a statement to the AFP news agency that Berlin would not “tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.
“Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out,” he said, adding that Hanning’s alleged actions would amount to “trampling his official duties underfoot”.
The current head of the BND, Martin Jaeger, told the German Rheinische Post newspaper that the agency had “quickly carried out extensive internal investigations” into the former chief before federal prosecutors took over the case.
“For the BND and for me, there are no compromises when it comes to internal security,” Jaeger said, adding that it had “not called into question any of my aims or any of my priorities”.
In 2023, a high-ranking German intelligence officer, identified as “Carsten L”, was charged with high treason when prosecutors alleged he had obtained classified intelligence on the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and shared it with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). His case is ongoing.
In 1974, West German Chancellor Willy Brandt was forced to resign following revelations that an East German spy had worked as his close aide for nearly two years.

articles.title_orig: Google’s Pixel Buds update will put them to sleep along with you
articles.title_zh: Google’s Pixel Buds update will put them to sleep along with you
articles.content_orig:
Plus new voice controls, and one-tap microphone muting and live translation, for the Buds 2A and Pro 2.
Plus new voice controls, and one-tap microphone muting and live translation, for the Buds 2A and Pro 2.
Google has detailed an update bringing a slew of new features to its Pixel Buds 2A and Pro 2 , which the company says are rolling out now. The new features were first teased in August .
The biggest update is Pixel Watch-powered sleep detection, rolling out to both pairs of earbuds. If you’re wearing a Pixel Watch, the buds will now react when you fall asleep, by pausing music, silencing notifications, and turning off touch controls.
Several other updates are also coming to both the Buds 2A and Pro. Tap-to-mute allows you to mute or unmute your microphone with a quick tap during calls, though only when also using a Pixel phone, and you can now activate live translation with a single tap. New Gemini voice commands will allow you to control active noise cancellation (ANC), adjust the EQ, or turn on touch controls.
The final new feature is Dynamic ANC, which will adjust audio and ANC levels based on the quality of the buds’ seal in your ears. This is exclusive to the Buds Pro 2.
Google announced the update rollout in a Pixel Buds community forum post . The original version of the announcement, posted yesterday, said that all the features except Dynamic ANC would also be coming to the original Pixel Buds Pro , but all mention of those earbuds has now been removed from the post. Pixel communications lead Natalie Johnson confirmed to The Verge that “these updates are not coming to the original Pixel Buds Pro.”
Update, October 7th: Added confirmation that the Pixel Buds Pro will not get the updates.

articles.title_orig: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.title_zh: Webb finds a surprising atmosphere on a scorching lava world
articles.content_orig:
For scientists searching for life beyond Earth, rocky planets with atmospheres are among the most promising places to investigate. An atmosphere is essential for maintaining liquid water on a planet's surface. Yet among the more than 6,300 exoplanets cataloged thus far, most are not rocky, and only a small number of known rocky planets appear to possess atmospheres.
Now, researchers have added another world to that short list. In a study published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , a team led by University of Chicago scientist Brandon Park Coy reports evidence of an atmosphere surrounding HD 3167 b, a rocky super-Earth located 154 light-years away in the constellation Pisces. The intensely hot planet, classified as a "lava world," completes an orbit around its star in only one Earth day.
"What's so surprising is that the closer a rocky planet orbits its star, the harder it should be to have an atmosphere, because it's bombarded by stellar wind and gets more high-energy photons from the star. But it seems that many of these lava worlds do," explained Edwin Kite, UChicago associate professor of geophysical sciences and co-author of the study. "These planets are too hot for life, but by studying them, we can say something about the processes that matter for other rocky worlds."
In the Q&A below,Coy, a graduate student in Kite's group and first author on the study, explains why atmospheres on lava worlds are scientifically valuable, how researchers detected evidence for this one, and what they hope to learn next.
What was the goal of the survey that found this atmosphere-bearing exoplanet?
One of the driving questions that the James Webb Space Telescope is being used to answer is whether planets orbiting stars much smaller than the sun have atmospheres. It appears that most of those terrestrial planets don't -- they're just bare rock.
But surprisingly, we've found evidence that the majority of lava worlds -- similar in composition to Earth and Venus but much, much hotter -- might have atmospheres. Five terrestrial planets found with atmospheres, including the one described in this study, have been ultra-hot.
This planet, however, is the coldest lava world found so far with evidence of an atmosphere. This is interesting because we're trying to understand the temperature transition between planets with and without atmospheres.
The result is the first from a program led by Megan Weiner Mansfield, PhD'21, who's now at the University of Maryland. The goal of the program, which is looking at 10 ultra-hot lava worlds, is to see if there's a critical temperature over which you start seeing planets with atmospheres.
"We're interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world." -- Study author Brandon Park Coy
How can you tell if an exoplanet has an atmosphere?
Right now, directly looking at Earth-like planets for signs of life is out of reach. Instead, we can use the Webb telescope to detect light in the mid-infrared wavelength range to estimate the temperature of exoplanets, which can tell us if they might have atmospheres.
There are two primary ways that we study exoplanets. One is called transit, when the planet goes in front of the host star. Another called secondary eclipse, which is the method we used for this study, is when the planet passes behind its star, and we can measure how much light is lost. That difference tells us how much mid-infrared light comes from the planet itself, which essentially tells us how hot the planet is.
If a planet doesn't have an atmosphere, its star-facing, day side should be as hot as theoretically possible based on how reflective its surface is and its distance from the star. But an atmosphere would help redistribute heat from the day side to the night side. We see this happen on Venus -- there's almost no difference in surface temperature between the day and night sides, or between the poles and the equator. If a planet has an atmosphere, it might also have clouds that reflect incoming starlight and cool the dayside. So if a planet's day side is cooler than the maximum possible, it likely has an atmosphere.
The subject of this study, HD 3167 b, is noticeably cooler than its expected maximum, providing strong evidence that it has an atmosphere.
What do you think HD 3167 b's atmosphere is made of?
These lava worlds are so-named because the surface facing their star is likely melted rock. We think that HD 3167 b might have a silicate-rich composition, with a similar mixture of minerals that make up Earth's mantle. Before this study, we expected that any atmosphere on these ultra-hot planets would be composed of vaporized rock, but we're starting to see evidence that some might have heavier gases like carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, or water in their atmospheres.
The makeup of HD 3167 b's atmosphere is still up in the air. That's one reason we're so interested in getting new observations.
Why is this result important?
Because the four other lava worlds found to have atmospheres are in the ultra-hot regime, it raises questions about whether there's a critical transition temperature when silicate atmospheres start becoming very thick. Is there a temperature where these planets form silicate cloud decks that might reflect incoming radiation to space and cool its day side? This relatively cooler planet helps us better characterize and nail down this transition.
Despite how inhospitable they are for life, we're also interested in studying these kinds of planets because we think early Earth might have looked a lot like a lava world. We think that very early in the solar system's history, when the terrestrial planets formed, they were extremely hot due to the energy from all of the planetesimal collisions. Earth had what's known as a magma ocean stage with an entirely liquid surface. This result gives us a window into studying what conditions may have been like in Earth's first couple of million years.
Materials provided by University of Chicago . Original written by Maureen Searcy. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title_orig: Collisions between dipolar molecules ‘switch off’ at low energies
articles.title_zh: Collisions between dipolar molecules ‘switch off’ at low energies
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
Researchers in the Netherlands have shown that they can turn off the dipole moment of molecules that are normally polar, drastically altering the molecules’ behaviour in low-energy collisions. The discovery – which was only possible after the team cleared a major experimental hurdle – has implications for ultracold chemistry and could also lead to a better understanding of polarity, with benefits for quantum simulation and computation.
Chemical reactions are full of complexity and chaos, making them hard to study at the atomic and molecular level. Before attempting to do so, scientists typically cool the reactants to just above absolute zero, which restricts their movement and vibrations. Despite these restrictions, however, interactions between ultracold molecules remain poorly understood, especially when the molecules have an electric dipole moment.
In 2023 experimental physicist Bas van de Meerakker and theorist colleagues at the Radboud University Nijmegen in the Netherlands shone a ray of light on this murky area by studying the collision cross-section (that is, the likelihood that collisions will take place) between molecules of ammonia (NH 3 ) at low energies. Their simulations showed that this cross-section falls off sharply as the energy decreases. This contradicts the classical picture of polarity, which suggests that the cross-section should continuously increase.
The Radboud team explained this discrepancy by noting that in the classical picture, polar molecules such as ammonia have a permanently asymmetric charge distribution – a dipole moment – due to the arrangement of the bonds between their constituent atoms. The quantum mechanical picture, in contrast, depicts an isolated molecule in a specific quantum state as having a definite parity, or symmetry. Because of this symmetry, the molecule’s net dipole moment in the lab frame is exactly zero.
According to this quantum picture, collisions between polar molecules at high speeds (high energies) cause these opposite parity states to mix via interactions between the molecules’ electrostatic fields. In the process, they essentially “turn on” each other’s dipole moments, causing them to attract each other and increasing the collision cross-section. At low speeds, however, the molecules cannot get close enough to trigger this mutual mixing. As a result, their dipole moments effectively switch off, and their collision rates drop drastically.
The Radboud team’s next step was to prove experimentally that this is indeed what happens. However, colliding cold molecules generally requires using electric fields to merge two molecular beams. When molecules in the two beams have very similar dipole moments, this is very difficult, because using an electric field to steer one beam automatically affects the path of the other. The risk is that the beams never overlap at all.
To overcome this obstacle, van de Meerakker and colleagues combined a 2.6 m Stark decelerator, a curved hexapole guide and a merged quadrupole/hexapole trap into a device that can overlap the beams at just the right position, with minimal angle between them. In this way, they achieved sufficient overlap to observe low-energy collisions. They then experimentally verified the predicted energy-dependent changes in cross-section for NH 3 -NH 3 collisions, while also showing that this dependence is different when they replace hydrogen atoms with deuterium (NH 3 -ND 3 or ND 3 -ND 3 collisions).
According to van de Meerakker, the fact that cross sections drop at low energies could make it hard to perform experiments that require scattering to take place in crossed or merged beams. On the other hand, experiments in which dipolar molecules are stored in traps could benefit, as lower inelastic cross-sections mean fewer molecules are lost from the trap.
As for future work, van de Meerakker says the team plans to add a controlled electric field to the beam overlap region. The mechanism they discovered is expected to respond extremely sensitively to this field, with even small electric fields changing cross sections by orders of magnitude and thereby providing a “knob” with which to control collision outcomes. “It was exactly this type of control that sparked our interest in cold and ultracold molecules two decades ago, and it is very exciting that this is now within reach in our scattering experiments,” van de Meerakker tells Physics World .
Quantum superchemistry emerges in the laboratory
Tim Langen , a physicist at Austria’s Vienna University of Technology who was not involved in this research, describes it as important because it provides experimental evidence for a phenomenon that had mainly been discussed theoretically. In his view, the results support the idea that effective dipolar interactions become strongly suppressed at low collision energies. He also finds the experimental approach “impressive” as it enables measurements in a regime that was previously difficult to access. “Overall, I find the work convincing and expect it to be of broad interest to researchers working on cold and ultracold molecules,” Langen concludes.
The research is published in Nature Chemistry .

articles.title_orig: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.title_zh: Bigger than Manhattan: The record-breaking airport megahub that conquered the world
articles.content_orig:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This CNN Travel series is, or was, sponsored by the country it highlights. CNN retains full editorial control over subject matter, reporting and frequency of the articles and videos within the sponsorship, in compliance with our policy .
Standing at the crossroad of continents, Istanbul has long been a global linchpin.
As Byzantium and then Constantinople, it controlled trade routes along the Silk Road and maritime passage from the Black Sea to the Mediterranean.
In the golden age of railways, Istanbul was the end point of the Orient Express, at the very cusp of Europe and Asia.
Now, in the 21st century, iGA Istanbul Airport is ruling the skies, having just overtaken London Heathrow as the best-connected airport on the planet.
“They’ve finally got the number one position,” says John Grant, chief analyst at OAG, a global travel data provider which has just released its Megahubs 2026 Index, comparing the world’s top airports.
The rankings are generated by comparing the number of scheduled connections to and from international flights , with the number of destinations served from the airport. They do this through a snapshot look at the busiest day of the year, which this year was August 2.
Gaining the top spot is “an important achievement for iGA Istanbul Airport and reflects the position we have built as a global aviation hub,” airport CEO Selahattin Bilgen tells CNN. “Today, we already serve approximately 350 destinations around the world, with significant room to grow further.”
Amsterdam Airport Schiphol is third place in this year’s ranking, followed by Kuala Lumpur at No.4 and Chicago O’Hare at No.5.
It’s been a swift and impressive rise for the award-winning $12 billion Istanbul Airport, which opened to much fanfare in 2018, about 20 miles outside Istanbul on the European side. This is a hub built for scale: Its huge 1.4-million-square-meter terminal is the world’s largest under one roof and the whole 76.5-million-square-meter site is bigger than Manhattan.
More than 84 million passengers pass through each year, making it the eighth busiest airport in the world. However, the long-term plan is to increase capacity to 200 million passengers per year, which is double the annual number currently handled by Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta, the world’s busiest airport.
“They’re going to be unassailable in the coming years,” says Grant. “They’ve got runway capacity. They’ve got a national airline that is hugely successful and continues to grow with new fleet orders. They’re very close to some of the most emergent markets in the world, such as Central Asia. They’ve benefited partly from the Middle East situation. They’re just very well placed.”
Istanbul Airport opened its fourth main runway last month and the end goal is for the hub to have nine: six main and three reserve.
The new  2,820-meter-long runway is its first to run east to west, meaning a reduction in taxiing and airborne times for westbound aircraft, saving time and fuel.
“They’re the only airport in the world that is licensed for three simultaneous runway operations,” says Grant, “You can build more frequency at those peak hours, and it gives you more operational flexibility. If you’ve got three runways, then you’re likely to improve your punctuality.”
Secrets of the sultan’s palace where concubines and eunuchs lived
Turkish Airlines has an 80% share of flights at Istanbul Airport and plays a key role in the hub’s success. Two years ago, it entered Guinness World Records for its achievement in flying to more countries than any other airline: 130 in total, as of 2026.
It operates a modern and rapidly expanding fleet of more than 500 Boeing and Airbus aircraft, including a diverse mix of narrow and widebody planes.
A younger fleet makes “a better impression” on customers, says Viktoriia Myroniuk, a senior lecturer in air transport management at the UK’s Cranfield University, reflecting on the polished service that helped earn Turkish Airlines its recent Skytrax award for Best Airline in Europe .
Newer aircraft are also more efficient, which, in this time of rising fuel prices, gives the airline a competitive edge, allowing them to lower ticket prices.
Selahattin Bilgen, CEO of iGA Istanbul Airport, tells CNN, “The efficiency and cost advantages we provide continue to attract new airlines to our network each year, and today we are one of only two major hubs worldwide serving the largest number of airlines.”
Infrastructure is equally key to that connectivity. “As a relatively new airport, iGA İstanbul Airport was designed from the outset with growth in mind, providing the capacity and flexibility to accommodate increasing passenger demand and support our role as a major international transfer hub.”
OAG’s 2026 Megahub rankings are inevitably affected by the ongoing disruption in the Middle East, as well as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
While other airports and regions have suffered, Istanbul Airport and Turkey’s geographical position and diplomatic relations have by chance granted it better fortune.
Istanbul Airport has the flexibility and capacity for growth that its competitors in the region lack. London Heathrow’s plan for a third runway remains highly controversial, due to the environmental impact in a highly built-up corner of southeast England. Amsterdam Schiphol, the world’s third best connected, has a flight cap of 488,000 movements a year.
“The fact that Istanbul Airport is slightly on the outskirts” means “they can operate 24/7,” says Myroniuk.
She also praises Turkish Airlines’ stopover program , which allows connecting passengers to take a break to explore Istanbul and enjoy free accommodation in partner hotels.
“I’m one of those unlucky passengers who really can’t sleep on board” and struggle on economy flights, Myroniuk says, but “your luggage stays with Turkish Airlines. You go to the perfect night’s rest.”
She married her brother, then he died. The monument to her grief was a Wonder of the Ancient World
It’s a form of sustainable tourism, she says, allowing travelers to embrace slower travel and to connect with local culture, rather than notching up cheap connecting flights with no experiences to show for it.
For many passengers it is also easier to get a visa to stop off in Turkey than it would be to take an exploratory tour from an EU airport, so that’s another advantage Istanbul Airport enjoys.
Although it’s hard to make any predictions in these turbulent times, Grant says that “all things being equal,” Istanbul will continue to hold onto its position in 2027.
“I think we’re going to see over the next three or four years the Chinese airports strengthen in their positions. We’re seeing more international growth from Chinese airlines, and that will help them,” he says.
International airlines including British Airways have yet to resume flying to the Middle East, but airports in the region will hopefully “get back to where they were,” says Grant. “All of which will continue to chip away at the position at Heathrow and Amsterdam Schiphol, and Paris, where we have European airports” that are reaching capacity.

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s sued for allegedly using AI tool to determine pricing for franchises
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s sued for allegedly using AI tool to determine pricing for franchises
articles.content_orig:
Suit says AI tool allows independently owned franchises to exchange nonpublic price and sales information
McDonald’s is facing a lawsuit in federal court over its alleged use of an AI tool to determine pricing across independent franchises, which prosecutors say violates antitrust laws and has unfairly inflated menu prices for Americans.
The vast majority of McDonald’s US stores are independently owned and are said to individually decide on prices under company policy. Antitrust laws require businesses to set prices independently from their competitors, as coordinating prices can stifle market competition and push up costs for consumers.
The lawsuit, filed on 2 October in a federal Chicago courtroom, alleges that McDonald’s AI tool is illegal because it amounts to independent franchise locations exchanging nonpublic price and sales data.
“This case is about McDonald’s bringing ‘optimization’ to America’s largest fast food chain,” the complaint says. “McDonald’s has built and for years deployed its own information-sharing pricing platform, which draws on data from its millions of daily transactions to set menu prices across thousands of US restaurants. The result is algorithmic price-fixing aimed at customers who are already stretched thin.”
In response to the lawsuit, a spokesperson for the McDonald’s corporation said that the “complaint is filled with inaccuracies and we will vigorously defend against this lawsuit”.
“AI does not set menu prices at McDonald’s restaurants – McDonald’s franchisees do,” it said. “Optional tools are available to franchisees to help them make the best decisions for their businesses and customers, but these tools do not automate, coordinate or fix pricing in any way.”
A recent Reuters investigation reported that some McDonald’s franchise owners have been pressured by the company to use the AI pricing tools and record their deviations from the tool’s recommendations. McDonald’s contested that characterization, calling the Reuters reporting “speculative and uninformed”.
The litigation, which has been proposed as a nationwide class-action lawsuit, was first brought forward by an Illinois man named Michael Thomas. Thomas, a McDonald’s regular who is described as “price conscious”, found that the cost of his usual order – a Quarter Pounder with cheese, fries and a Coke – varied even within his neighborhood in DeKalb, Illinois. The attorney listed as representing Thomas did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Thomas does not appear to be alone in his experience. At a McDonald’s in Manhattan’s financial district, Chukwama Okeke, 43, was finishing a mango-pineapple smoothie that he bought as part of a value meal that cost about $15 – something he only gets about once a month.
Okeke said that when he orders the same meal at a McDonald’s in Brooklyn’s Crown Heights neighborhood, he ends up paying closer to $9.
“McDonald’s in Manhattan is much more expensive than those in Brooklyn,” he said. “I’ve notice in some areas if they have a lot of like foot traffic, the prices tend to get higher.”
Beatriz Milander, 27, who ordered a snack wrap, a small fries and an iced coffee for $11.51, hadn’t noticed a huge difference between what she pays in the financial district and what she pays in her Bronx neighborhood, but said prices overall had inched up.
“In the last few months, I’ve seen them do more deals or like lower-priced things,” she said. “But it definitely was pricing up for a little bit there.”
Experts say that companies using AI to set or alter pricing could exacerbate the country’s affordability crisis and make it harder for Americans to bear everyday costs. So far this year, at least 90 pieces of legislation have been filed across the country to push back against algorithmic price-fixing, according to Lindsay Owens, the head of the left-leaning thinktank Groundwork Collaborative, who recently authored a book on the topic.
McDonald’s acquired an AI company, Dynamic Yield, in 2019, but has firmly denied using AI in setting menu prices. In a statement released on 1 October, the day before the lawsuit was filed, the chain denied using dynamic pricing and described its pricing tool as simply providing information that franchises are free to decide whether to adopt.
The fast-food chain has been scrutinized over recent years for its elevated prices, and went viral in 2023 over an $18 Big Mac meal at a Connecticut McDonald’s. The franchise’s owner filed a lawsuit alleging that it was the AI pricing tool that suggested the $18 price to the franchise.
According to a fact sheet the chain published in 2024, the average price of a McDonald’s menu item increased about 40% between 2019 and 2024.

New information reveals that, over the weekend, the U.S. removed all long-range bombers from the British air base near where five men were arrested last week in a suspected terror plot. High school students in France are blocking schools today , after hundreds of thousands of them marched across the country yesterday. They are joined by teachers, parents and labor union members. The movement, which began in a particularly run-down high school facing teacher absenteeism, aims to improve learning conditions and address inequalities in the French education system.
A former head of Germany's foreign intelligence agency will appear before a federal judge today to face charges of espionage and attempted treason. Federal prosecutors accuse August Hanning of using classified information to brief a foreign intelligence agency. He served as the head of Germany's CIA equivalent for seven years from 1998 to 2005. Prosecutors allege he shared sensitive political information for 12 years after leaving office. They have not yet disclosed who Hanning's alleged clients were.
As Israel marks three years since Hamas' surprise Oct. 7 attacks , new reports in Israeli and U.S. media say regional allies warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that Hamas was planning to attack. Four people in the Middle East with direct knowledge of the warnings told NPR that Netanyahu was personally informed about the potential attacks and his security agencies were notified multiple times in the weeks and days leading up to Oct. 7, 2023. Netanyahu has denied this, labeling the reports "fake news" and recently filing a defamation lawsuit against the news outlets that first published the information. He and his defense minister now warn that Hamas might attempt to attack again on this Oct. 7 memorial day and leading up to Israel's national elections later this month.

articles.title_orig: How Israeli and Palestinian kids are coping 3 years after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks ignited the Middle East
articles.title_zh: How Israeli and Palestinian kids are coping 3 years after the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks ignited the Middle East
articles.content_orig:
Three years after Hamas militants launched their assault on southern Israel, killing 1,200 people, taking 251 others hostage and triggering Israel's war in Gaza that has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians, CBS News met two teenagers on both sides of the Gaza border to find out how they are coping.
Ron Shargian, 15, said growing up in southern Israel has meant learning to live with fear. He was 12 when he watched Hamas militants on paragliders soar over a wall meant to protect his community.
"It feels like some kind of nightmare," he told CBS News three years later, calling the experience on that fateful day surreal, "and something I wouldn't believe if anyone told me it's going to happen."
The attackers killed 17 of his neighbors in Netiv HaAsara, the Israeli community that was closest to the Gaza border.
As the assault unfolded, he and his family locked themselves inside their home's bomb shelter.
"Every time the gunshots get close to you, you think that that's the end, that they're coming to your house now," he recalled.
His family escaped after 11 hours, when security forces came to the rescue, but like thousands of other Israelis displaced by the war, they couldn't go back home, at least not right away.
After Oct. 7, Shargian's family lived in a hotel for evacuees, and then in Tel Aviv, and then in another hotel, and then a year and a half in the coastal town of Gan Yavne. Finally, a little over a year ago, his family returned to their home.
"It was really hard to come back," he said. "But I also anticipated it very much. I really missed my home, my friends, the community — it's something that you don't have anywhere else."
Across the border in Gaza, safe places have been hard for Palestinian children to find since Israel launched its full-scale military assault in retaliation for the Hamas attack.
"Lots of things has been destroyed for me," Kazem Doghmash told CBS News. He was 11 when the war started.
Israel pummeled Gaza for years with daily airstrikes in a grueling war that, despite a cease-fire in place since last October ending major combat, continues to claim lives three years later . Palestinian officials in Gaza say more than 1,400 people have been killed in Gaza since the cease-fire officially came into effect.
"They say a lot of times that the war will finish, but the war has been not finished, the war has been more difficult," said Doghmash, who is now 14.
"Before the war, I am just being a kid," he said, remembering it as "a good life."
In Israel, Shargian said he struggles with how to think about people on the other side of the Gaza border after everything that happened.
"I don't know if there are good people there," he said. "Up until October 7th, I thought that we could make peace. But from that day, something inside me broke."
He is trying to move forward and lead a normal teenage life — learning the guitar, hanging out with friends at the beach, and he told CBS News the wider conflict now engulfing the Middle East can, at times, even feel distant.
"I don't think we feel the war so much, like, it's in other countries," he said.
When the sound of a rocket or an air raid siren jolts him back to reality, he said like most Israelis, he takes it in his stride.
"Because we're so used to this reality," he said. "So, we just don't make a big deal out of it."
But even though it has happened throughout his life, he said he still feels it inside, every time he and his family or friends hear an alarm and have to rush for shelter.
"Your muscles get tight and you have an adrenaline rush," he said. "It's something we just got used to."
Moving forward has been hard for Doghmash, too. He still can't think about returning to normal teenage pursuits.
"My life has been destroyed," he said. "My school has been destroyed, a lot of things have been destroyed for me."
"We are focusing [on] how we're going to live," he said.
But he hasn't given up on his dreams. He told CBS News he hopes to become a doctor, and he has resumed studying at the British International School in Gaza —   in its new location, as the original building was destroyed by Israeli airstrikes —   where his favorite subject is English.
As he led CBS News through the rubble of what used to be his family's home, he longed for anything resembling a return to his life before the war.
"We need to live in a good life, not to just, thinking how we're gonna get food and the water," he said. "We're gonna need to go to school, to go, to be happy and smile."
The United Nations Children's Fund says more than 21,000 Palestinian children have been reported killed in Gaza since Oct. 7, 2023, as a result of Israel's counteroffensive.
Dozens of Israeli children have died, too, including 37 killed in the initial Hamas attacks.
Despite everything they've been through, both boys are still finding moments in life to just be kids.

On 25 September 2026, World Lung Day highlighted the importance of respiratory health as a public health priority, calling for stronger prevention, earlier detection, equitable access to care and healthier environments.
Respiratory diseases remain a major public health challenge across Europe. While many lung diseases are preventable, addressing their impact requires coordinated action from policymakers, healthcare professionals, researchers and communities.
This year’s message, “Healthy Lungs, Healthy Populations,” emphasised the need to translate scientific evidence into effective public health action.
These priorities closely align with the objectives of the Joint Action on Respiratory Diseases (JARED), which brings together European partners to improve respiratory health, strengthen prevention and reduce health inequalities.
World Lung Day serves as a reminder that protecting lung health requires sustained commitment and collaboration across sectors.
Better policies. Stronger health systems. Healthier lungs.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia RTX Spark for $2,999.99: HP leak reveals RTX Spark laptop pricing ahead of launch
articles.title_zh: Nvidia RTX Spark for $2,999.99: HP leak reveals RTX Spark laptop pricing ahead of launch
articles.content_orig:
HP unveiled the RTX Spark-powered OmniBook Ultra 16 and OmniBook X 14 at IFA 2026, both set to be offered with either the lower-end chip with a 5120-core GPU and an 18-core CPU or the full-fat variant with a 6144-core GPU and a 20-core CPU. HP didn't reveal pricing or exact launch dates for the two laptops at the time, but we now have a better idea of how much they'll cost.
The company briefly listed both laptops on its US online store, revealing much higher starting prices than anticipated. To recap, RTX Spark-powered laptops were tipped to start at $1,799 with the lower-end chip and around $2,899 with the higher-end version. However, HP is planning to offer the 14-inch OmniBook X starting at $2,999.99 and $3,199.99 for the 16-inch OmniBook Ultra, according to the listings. That includes the lower-end RTX Spark chip, 32GB of LPDDR5x-9400 unified memory, and a 1TB PCIe Gen 5 SSD.
The listings also showed that both laptops can be configured with the higher-end RTX Spark and up to 128GB of unified memory. Preconfigured models with the 6144-core GPU and a 20-core CPU variant were listed at $4,499.99 for the OmniBook X 14 and $4,999.99 for the OmniBook Ultra 16, including 64GB of RAM and a 2TB SSD.
It's still unclear when HP will release the RTX Spark-powered OmniBook Ultra 16 and OmniBook X 14, but Microsoft is expected to launch a new Surface laptop with Nvidia RTX Spark on October 7. That's a day ahead of MSI and Asus , both of which are expected to open orders for their own models on October 8 in China.
That said, with the leaked HP pricing, RTX Spark will be the most expensive Windows-on-ARM platform. By comparison, Snapdragon-powered laptops can be had for $1,999.99 with the powerful Snapdragon X2 Elite chip and 32GB RAM or as low as $599.99, including HP's own Snapdragon X-powered OmniBook 3 ( curr: $599.99 on Amazon ). Joseph Chee , CEO and Chairman of Solana Company (NASDAQ: HSDT ), said on Tuesday that China is “very closely” monitoring cryptocurrency and blockchains, while continuing to have reservations about how the technology is used.
During an interview with CNBC, Chee said that there are Chinese think tanks, academics and other groups who are familiar with the technology.
Chee, formerly head of UBS Asia investment banking and with extensive experience in China, said officials are still “very worried” about ordinary people getting exploited by the new technology.
“But they know that’s not the technology they can ignore,” he added.
Chee said China is using Hong Kong as a testing ground for how cryptocurrency-related systems might be implemented and managed.
Notably, Hong Kong is a growing hub for digital asset innovation, wealth and talent, ranking as one of the world’s most cryptocurrency-friendly cities
Chee said China should prioritise education first, so that those responsible for managing cryptocurrency fully “understand how to manage” the technology before any wider rollout.
He said that China could continue restricting cryptocurrency trading and stablecoin issuance on the mainland, while allowing blockchain tools to support business and government operations.

Beijing issued multiple restrictions between 2013 and 2021 that ultimately banned all cryptocurrency transactions and mining. China’s central bank formally declared all digital-asset trading illegal in September 2021, and providing such services to Chinese citizens from abroad is also prohibited.
The central bank reaffirmed the enforcement last year, voicing specific worries about dollar-pegged stablecoins. Instead. Instead, China has focused on advancing its central bank digital currency , the Digital Yuan.

articles.title_orig: Greetings abound as Bossey turns 80
articles.title_zh: Greetings abound as Bossey turns 80
articles.content_orig:
Global religious leaders shared greetings during the celebration of the 80th anniversary of the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey on 7 October.
His All-Holiness Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew video message being presented during the commemorations of the 80th anniversary of Bossey.
His All-Holiness Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, in a video message, expressed affection for the institute, recalling his own studies there.
“Since October 1946, the Chateau de Bossey has welcomed students from every Christian  tradition and from every corner of the world,” he said. “ It is fitting therefore that this anniversary should be marked by the gathering of Bossey ’ s alumnae and alumni, for they are the truest measure of what these 80 years have accomplished.”
Cardinal Kurt Koch, prefect of the Dicastery for Promoting Christian Unity, in a written greeting, noted that the history of Bossey is closely interwoven with the deepening relationship between the Catholic Church and the World Council of Churches. “ The establishment of the Joint Working Group in 1965, the first meeting of which was held at Bossey in May 1965, opened a new and enduring chapter of dialogue and practical cooperation, ” he wrote. “ Bossey soon became one of its particularly fruitful expressions.”
H.E. Metropolitan Anthony, chairman of the Department for External Church Relations of the Moscow Patriarchate, in a written greeting, reflected that a number of Russian Orthodox Church representatives have gained invaluable experience of inter-Christian dialogue at Bossey.
“ I would also like to mention high academic standards maintained by the Ecumenical Institute at Bossey, which implements its educational programs in collaboration with the University of Geneva,” he wrote. “ On this memorable occasion, I wish you God's help and blessed success in your further ministry.”
Most Rev. Dr Olav Fykse Tveit, presiding bishop of the Church of Norway, expressed deep thanks for all that Bossey represents and continues to offer as a place of study and reflection, a space where people from different traditions and backgrounds come together in dialogue, and a living symbol of the ecumenical movement.
“ Over the years, Bossey has been much more than an academic institution,” said Tveit. “ It has been a place of encounter, friendship, learning, and transformation—a place where differences can be explored with openness and respect, and where the shared calling to build greater understanding and unity can take root.”

articles.title_orig: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.title_zh: California pair charged with abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children
articles.content_orig:
A California pair has been charged with multiple counts of abusing at least 14 surrogate-born children - some as young as two months old - and dissuading a witness.
"The number of children who were subjected to this alleged horrific abuse is unprecedented," Los Angeles District Attorney Nathan J Hochman said in a statement.
Guojun Xuan and Silvia Zhang, who US media describe as a couple, were arrested at their Arcadia mansion on Tuesday.
The pair pleaded not guilty at a Pasadena courthouse, the BBC's US partner CBS News reported.
Xuan, 66, and Zhang, 39, are accused of conspiring to subject 15 of the 16 children living in their home to repeated physical abuse, after 21 children were removed from their custody last year.
The pair ran their own surrogacy company and are accused of making false statements to at least two women who became surrogates, indicating that Zhang was struggling to conceive, according to the criminal complaint.
As of May 2025, Zhang maintained a spreadsheet that tracked 21 children, including those born to surrogates.
Officials said the investigation began that month when Zhang brought a two-month-old boy to the hospital with a head injury, telling medical staff that the baby had fallen from a bed.
The couple's lawyer Mitchell Krems said the allegation was a "mischaracterisation" based on the evidence he has reviewed, CBS News in Los Angeles reported.
Hospital staff informed law enforcement, and when police arrived at their home they discovered three different rooms called "learning centres" under the supervision of multiple nannies, which Hochman described as a "house of horrors".
The mansion allegedly had 32 motion-activated cameras which Hochman said were used by the couple to monitor the discipline given by the nannies.
Footage allegedly shows the nannies spanking, slapping or hitting the children.
One nanny, Chunmei Li, is accused of hitting the two-month-old baby who suffered the head injury two days before he was brought to the hospital.
Krems said Li was quickly fired, CBS News LA reported.
Li, 58, was previously charged with one felony count of child abuse under conditions likely to cause great bodily injury or death. Hochman said she was on the run with a $105,000 (£88,800) warrant for her arrest.
In July 2025, the couple's home was first raided by authorities, who took 21 children into state custody.
Arcadia Police Department said at the time the couple's house was first raided that the children ranged in age from two months to 13 years old, but most were between one and three years old.
Fifteen of the children were taken from the couple's home while six others were living elsewhere and also later taken into custody.
Krems said his client Xuan was innocent.
"He is being targeted for exercising his constitutional right to have a large family," CBS News quoted the lawyer as saying.
Investigators believe the surrogate mothers were from around the country and they were unaware they were carrying embryos for the couple at the same time.
Melissa Brisman, the attorney for two of the surrogates, told CBS News: "This is wonderful news that people will be held responsible for their actions and there will be consequences if you abuse the surrogacy system".
If convicted as charged, Xuan faces a possible maximum sentence of 17 years and four months in state prison, while Zhang faces up to 11 years and eight months. Li faces up to 12 years.
